doc.title: Howard Johnson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

title: Ernie Wilkins, Gil Evans and low-voice colors
summary: Phoning Ernie Wilkins led to his first recording; Gil Evans called after seeing him with Mingus, writing for tuba and bass clarinet.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Well I was looking for him around the same time I was looking for Mingus, because all I wanted to do was meet these guys you know. Ernie Wilkins, who did the great arrangement of “Every Day I Have the Blues,” I met him someplace, and he actually said he didn’t use tuba anymore. And I said, “Well you have to hear me.” He said, “Well fine.” He’d given the tuba to use in every context and it was all right much of the time but it was mostly wanting. So he didn’t want to hear me play. So I got his phone number and called him up and his wife put him on the phone and I held the mic up here and the phone up here and started jamming. When I stopped I pulled the phone down and he was still laughing. He says, “Okay, man, give me your number.”
Oh that’s great. © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

And that was my first recording, was with Ernie Wilkins. But I spotted Gil Evans one night when I was playing with Mingus at the Five Spot. I thought oh, here’s my chance — it’s been two years and I haven’t been able to find this guy. So I put my instrument up and came back out and he had left. I said oh no is it going to be another two years before I see him? But he called me about a couple of weeks later because he’d gotten my number from Mingus.
Well he knew how to deal with the potential clash between the bass and the tuba it seems.
And the bass clarinet was in there too.
It gave him about six different colors to use for the low notes. Sometimes the tuba was too heavy for the woodwinds but the bass clarinet is just right.
